newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Rivals plan first Bosnian parliament session.
newsitem.headline: Rivals plan first Bosnian parliament session.

text.p: Bosnia's inter-ethnic presidency agreed on Monday to set the first peacetime session of parliament for January 3, ending weeks of obstruction by Serb leaders.

The parliament, which was elected in polls held last September, is supposed to govern Moslem-Croat and Serb sectors of Bosnia but has yet to convene because of manoeuvring and stalling by former combatants, mainly Serbs.

But on Monday the collective presidency, which includes Serb nationalist leader Momcilo Krajisnik, Moslem president Alija Izetbegovic and Croat representative Kresimir Zubak, announced it wanted parliament to meet on Friday.
The Bosnian Serbs had linked their attendance to the parliament to objections over the venue for cabinet meetings.
The impasse was resolved after the Serbs backed an agreement in which the cabinet meetings would alternate between Serb and Moslem-Croat federation territory.

The accord worked out between the co-chairs of the cabinet, known as the council of ministers, paved the way for the parliament session, said Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia.
"I think this is good news," Steiner told reporters.
Steiner, who helped mediate the discussions, had accused the Serb side last week of obstructing efforts to form a central post-war government for Bosnia.
He recommended a "time out" in negotiations for several days after last week's talks collapsed.
Diplomats had warned the Bosnian Serbs they would miss out on vital reconstruction aid if they blocked joint governing bodies devised to reunite the country after 3-1/2 years of war.
"Apparently they (Serb leaders) have realised that in the end they would hurt mainly the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina if they insist on something which cannot lead to a consensus," Steiner said.
Krajisnik and the Serb leadership had demanded the new cabinet meet more frequently on Serb territory.

The House of Representatives will hold its first working session in Sarajevo on Friday and the parliament's upper chamber, the House of Peoples, will also convene on Friday in the Serb-controlled suburb of Lukavica.
The parliament is expected to confirm nominations for the small cabinet, which is comprised of foreign affairs, foreign trade and communications ministries.
The presidency has proposed nominees to head the three ministries, distributing the posts among the country's Moslem, Serb and Croat communities.
Jadranko Prlic, a Croat and outgoing foreign minister for Bosnia's wartime government, has been nominated to continue as foreign minister.

Parliament has never held a full session since separatist Serb deputies boycotted an inaugural ceremony in October in Sarajevo, citing concerns over the venue and the text of an oath of allegiance to Bosnian statehood.
Steiner said the Serbs' parliamentary leader has since signed the oath and the other deputies are expected to follow suit.

The presidency has called on the cabinet to work out a permanent venue for its meetings. One proposal under consideration would create a special district in Sarajevo where joint government institutions would be located.
